result:
I would give every person—and every institution we build—a reliably “on-demand” capacity for informed empathy.

Why that, out of all possibilities?

1. Root-cause leverage  
   – Most large-scale problems (violence, corruption, extreme inequality, climate apathy, misinformation, prejudice) persist because we discount the experiences of people outside our immediate circle or timeframe.  
   – When we vividly grasp how our choices land on strangers, future generations, and non-human life, many downstream issues become solvable with the tools we already possess.

2. Self-correcting side effects  
   – Empathy that is paired with good information naturally pressures societies toward fairer laws, transparent governance, sustainable production, and collaborative science.  
   – It also acts as a guardrail against fanaticism: the moment a belief system begins harming others, the empathetic feedback loop flags it.

3. Scalability  
   – Technologies, policies, and cultural norms can embed empathy (e.g., citizen assemblies, impact disclosures on products, virtual-reality perspective taking, empathy-training in schools). Once seeded, these mechanisms reinforce one another.

What the world would likely look like:

• Conflict resolution first, force second.  
• Economic engines tuned for shared prosperity instead of zero-sum extraction.  
• Rapid, coordinated action on climate and bio-diversity because the costs to others become emotionally “real.”  
• Algorithms and media audited for how they affect collective well-being, not just engagement metrics.  
• An education system that trains citizens to ask, “Who isn’t in the room and how are they affected?”

No single change is a silver bullet, but a widespread, teachable skill of stepping into another’s shoes—while remaining analytically rigorous—gives humanity its best chance to tackle any other challenge it encounters.
